action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'pin', 'unpin'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

edits.description: publish: small changes Claude makes to the file at `file_path` in this same call, instead of editing the file with Edit and publishing after. Use it on a page (add `url` to update an artifact from another conversation). Not allowed with `files`. Each old_str is text copied exactly from the file as it now stands and must occur in it exactly once; new_str takes its place (empty deletes it). The edits apply in order, all or none: the file is published with them and then saved with them on disk, so it stays the source for later changes; on a miss nothing is changed or published, and the result says which edit failed and why.

old_str.description: Text copied exactly from the file; must occur once.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all' and 'files' (with `url`). See **Calls**.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

# Installation

## Python (pyenv)

This project requires Python 3.12 (`requires-python = ">=3.12, <3.13"`). The exact
version is pinned in `.python-version`, so pyenv and uv agree on it.

```sh
brew install pyenv
pyenv install            # builds the version pinned in .python-version
pyenv global 3.12.9      # optional: default interpreter outside this repo
```

Put the shims on `PATH` in `~/.zshenv` (every shell) and initialise pyenv in
`~/.zshrc` (interactive shells):

```sh
export PYENV_ROOT="$HOME/.pyenv"
export PATH="$PYENV_ROOT/shims:$PATH"
eval "$(pyenv init -)"
```

`[tool.uv]` in `pyproject.toml` pins uv to the pyenv interpreter
(`python-preference = "only-system"`, `python-downloads = "never"`), so uv never
silently downloads a second, unpinned Python.

## Install Dependencies
Install uv

Run `uv sync`

`certifi` and `virtualenv` are pinned at versions carrying the fix for the
October 2026 eMudhra/emSign CA incident
(<https://discuss.python.org/t/information-for-python-users-regarding-emudhra-emsign-ca-certificate-security-incident/109576>).
Keep `pip >= 26.2.2` and `certifi >= 2026.10.19` in any environment you create
outside uv.

## Download audio model

uv run moonshine-voice download --stt --language en

Note down the model path

export MOONSHINE_MODEL_PATH=path_to_your_model

content.text:
Both big models are better than I expected: 262k context, native **tools + thinking**, and qwen3.8:27b even has thinking levels. But 262k is the *model's* ceiling — your hardware's ceiling is much lower, and it's set by the KV cache, not the weights.

## The real constraint: KV cache math on 24 GB

| Setup | Weights | KV cache @ 32k ctx | + voice stack & OS | Fits? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| qwen3.8:27b (dense) | 17 GB | ~8 GB fp16 (~4 GB q8) | +7–9 GB | ❌ Swaps badly |
| MiniCPM-V-35B-A3B (MoE) | 16 GB | ~2–3 GB (smaller dims) | +7–9 GB | ⚠️ Marginal, ctx ≤16k |
| MiniCPM5-2B | 1.6 GB | <1 GB | +7–9 GB | ✅ Easily, but weak agent |

Dense 27B + long context + concurrent agents simply does not fit in 24 GB alongside the voice stack. And even if it fit, prefill of a 30k-token context on an M4 takes tens of seconds per agent turn.

## The architecture that actually works: split the context, don't grow it

"Longer context" for a multi-agent harness is better solved structurally — give each agent a **focused 4–16k context** (the coding agent gets the repo slice it needs, the search agent gets query+results) and have an **orchestrator hold only summaries**. That's the pattern real harnesses (including this one) use: total information processed is huge, but no single context blows the memory budget.

Recommended assignment:

| Role | Model | Why |
|---|---|---|

content.text:
`/loop` is Claude Code's skill for **recurring tasks** — it runs a prompt or slash command repeatedly instead of once. It has two modes:

## 1. Fixed interval — `/loop 5m <prompt or /command>`

```text
/loop 5m check the deploy status
/loop 30m /babysit-prs
/loop 2h pull latest main and run the test suite
```

The task fires on a schedule (minutes/hours/days). Each firing re-runs the prompt or slash command as a fresh turn. Good for polling external state — CI runs, deploys, queues.

## 2. Dynamic (self-paced) — `/loop <prompt>` with no interval

```text
/loop keep refactoring until the test suite is clean
```

Here Claude schedules its own wake-ups via a `ScheduleWakeup` mechanism, choosing the delay based on what it's waiting for — short intervals when actively polling something, longer heartbeats when idle. The loop keeps going until the task is done or you stop it.

## How it behaves

- **Runs in your session** — each iteration is a new turn with the accumulated context, so the model remembers what happened last cycle
- **Quiet cycles collapse** — consecutive "nothing changed" ticks are compressed in the terminal view so long idle holds stay readable without scrolling
- **Interruptible** — you can stop it anytime by just telling Claude to stop the loop (or interrupting the session)
- **Best for**: watching PRs, polling deploys, babysitting background jobs, "keep doing X until Y" workflows
- **Not for**: one-off tasks — just ask directly instead

Given the harness idea from earlier: `/loop` is a lightweight way to prototype the orchestrator pattern — e.g. `/loop 10m review open PRs and summarize blockers` — though a real multi-agent harness would use the Agent/Workflow tooling instead. Want me to set one up for something?

# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID).
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `timeout_ms: 1800000`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. A monitor expires after at most 30 minutes and tells you; on later iterations call TaskList first and re-arm only if no monitor for it is still running.
3. **Decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   - `noop`: `true` if this tick changed nothing ("still waiting", "quiet hold"); `false` if it did something worth keeping. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks collapse in the terminal.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
4. **After the wakeup is armed, briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you picked. This must be ordinary visible response text — the user cannot see your thinking/reasoning, so an update written only there is invisible to them. Make it the last thing in the turn, then end the turn.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from the schedule step above (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat), then write the same brief update as visible text. If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Then write the loop's outcome for the user as ordinary visible response text — a stopped loop has no next tick to surface it. Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop.

import numpy as np
import sounddevice as sd
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from kokoro import KPipeline

from lib.chat import Chat
from lib.openrouter import OpenRouterProvider

AGENT_SPEAKER = 1
SAMPLE_RATE = 24000
MAX_TOKENS = 150
TIMEOUT = 5
SESSION_ID = str(uuid.uuid4())
LANG_CODE = "a"  # American english, use English as models work better
MODEL = "google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite"  # Use a low latency model
VOICE = "af_heart"

DEFAULT_PROMPT = """You're an AI assistant.
The user is dictating you messages through an ASR model. Expect errors from the transcription model.
Below you'll have the entire chat history from this session.

Try to respond as succintly and naturally as possible, assume this is a voice chat.

USE ONLY ONE SENTENCE AT A TIME.

EXCEPT WHEN EXPLICITLY ASKED OTHERWISE BY THE USER.

Try to keep word count as low as possible, and let user guide the direction of the chat.

When facing with ambiguity, ask the user back with the least amount of words, like a human.

import multiprocessing as mp

from lib.api_pipeline import ApiPipeline
from lib.audio_pipeline import AudioPipeline, AudioPipelineConfig
from lib.event_aggregation_pipeline import EventAggregationPipeline
from lib.moonshine_pipeline import MoonshineRealTimePipeline
from lib.nemotron_pipeline import NemotronRealTimePipeline

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Create base queues for inter-process communication
    mp.set_start_method("spawn")

    event_queue = mp.Queue()
    aggregated_event_queue = mp.Queue()
    nemotron_audio_queue = mp.Queue()
    moonshine_audio_queue = mp.Queue()

    # Create processes
    audio_pipeline_config = AudioPipelineConfig()  # use default values
    audio_pipeline_process = mp.Process(
        target=AudioPipeline.start_audio_pipeline,
        args=(
            [nemotron_audio_queue, moonshine_audio_queue],
            audio_pipeline_config,
        ),
    )
    nemotron_process = mp.Process(
        target=NemotronRealTimePipeline.start_nemotron,
        args=(
            nemotron_audio_queue,
            audio_pipeline_config,
            event_queue,
        ),
    )
    moonshine_process = mp.Process(
        target=MoonshineRealTimePipeline.start_moonshine,
        args=(
            moonshine_audio_queue,
            audio_pipeline_config,
            event_queue,
        ),
    )
    event_aggregation_process = mp.Process(
        target=EventAggregationPipeline.start_event_aggregation,
        args=(
            event_queue,
            aggregated_event_queue,
        ),
    )
    api_process = mp.Process(
        target=ApiPipeline.start_api_sync, args=(aggregated_event_queue,)
    )
    created_processes = [
        ("audio_pipeline", audio_pipeline_process),
        ("nemotron", nemotron_process),
        ("moonshine", moonshine_process),
        ("event_aggregation", event_aggregation_process),
        ("api_process", api_process),
    ]

    # Start processes
    for name, p in created_processes:
        p.start()

    # TODO: implement stop event handling
    keep_running = True
    while keep_running:
        for p_name, p in created_processes:
            if not p.is_alive():
                print(f"process {p} died")
                keep_running = False

import os
import queue

import numpy as np
from moonshine_voice import ModelArch, Transcriber, TranscriptEventListener

from lib.audio_pipeline import AudioPipelineConfig
from lib.segments import ASRSegmentEvent


class MoonshineRealTimePipeline:
    def __init__(
        self,
        input_audio_queue: queue.Queue,
        audio_pipeline_config: AudioPipelineConfig,
        output_event_queue: queue.Queue,
    ):
        # TODO: use input audio queue and audio pipeline config
        self.input_audio_queue = input_audio_queue
        self.output_event_queue = output_event_queue
        self.model_path = os.environ["MOONSHINE_MODEL_PATH"]
        self.model_arch = ModelArch.MEDIUM_STREAMING
        self.audio_pipeline_config = audio_pipeline_config

        if audio_pipeline_config.dtype != "float32":
            raise ValueError(
                f"Moonshine pipeline does not support this dtype: {audio_pipeline_config.dtype}"
            )

        self.transcriber = Transcriber(
            model_path=self.model_path,
            model_arch=self.model_arch,
        )
        self.transcriber.add_listener(ASRListener(self.output_event_queue))

    def run_loop(self):
        self.transcriber.start()
        print("Moonshine Ready")
        print("*" * 50)
        try:
            while True:
                audio_block = self.input_audio_queue.get()
                self.transcriber.add_audio(
                    np.asarray(audio_block, dtype=np.float32),
                    self.audio_pipeline_config.sample_rate,
                )
        finally:
            self.transcriber.stop()

    @classmethod
    def start_moonshine(
        cls,
        input_audio_queue: queue.Queue,
        audio_pipeline_config: AudioPipelineConfig,
        output_event_queue: queue.Queue,
    ):
        """Starts ASR pipeline."""
        MoonshineRealTimePipeline(
            input_audio_queue=input_audio_queue,
            audio_pipeline_config=audio_pipeline_config,
            output_event_queue=output_event_queue,
        ).run_loop()


class ASRListener(TranscriptEventListener):
    def __init__(self, output_event_queue: queue.Queue):
        super().__init__()
        self.output_event_queue = output_event_queue

    def on_line_completed(self, event):
        line = event.line

        event = ASRSegmentEvent(
            start=line.start_time,
            end=line.start_time + line.duration,
            text=line.text,
        )
        self.output_event_queue.put(event.as_dict())

while True:
            block = self.input_audio_queue.get()
            buffer = np.concatenate((buffer, block))
            total += len(block)

            while True:
                first = mel_frame_idx is None
                if first:
                    start, end = 0, p.num_samples_first_audio_chunk
                else:
                    start = p.audio_chunk_start(mel_frame_idx)
                    end = start + p.num_samples_per_audio_chunk
                if total < end:
                    break  # not enough audio yet

                chunk = buffer[start - buffer_start : end - buffer_start]
                inputs = p(
                    chunk,
                    sampling_rate=self.sample_rate,
                    is_streaming=True,
                    is_first_audio_chunk=first,
                )
                inputs = inputs.to(self.model.device, dtype=self.model.dtype)
                with torch.inference_mode():
                    outputs = self.model(**inputs, speaker_cache=speaker_cache)
                speaker_cache = outputs.speaker_cache

                logits = outputs.logits.cpu()
                self.logits_to_segment_events(logits, frames_done, open_segments)
                frames_done += logits.shape[1]

                step = p.num_mel_frames_per_step
                mel_frame_idx = step if first else mel_frame_idx + step

                next_start = p.audio_chunk_start(
                    mel_frame_idx
                )  # drop audio nobody needs again
                buffer = buffer[next_start - buffer_start :]
                buffer_start = next_start

    def logits_to_segment_events(self, logits, frames_done, open_segments):
        """Converting state into emitted raw events."""
        t0 = frames_done * FRAME_S
        t1 = t0 + logits.shape[1] * FRAME_S
        segs = self.processor.extract_speaker_dict(logits)[0]
        seen = {s["Speaker"] for s in segs}

        for s in segs:
            speaker = s["Speaker"]
            start, end = t0 + s["Start"], t0 + s["End"]  # absolute times

            # the old segment ended before this chunk
            if speaker in open_segments and s["Start"] > EPS:
                self.emit(
                    SpeakerSegmentState.closed, speaker, open_segments.pop(speaker), t0
                )

            if speaker not in open_segments:
                open_segments[speaker] = start
                self.emit(SpeakerSegmentState.open, speaker, start)

            # stopped inside this chunk
            if end < t1 - EPS:
                self.emit(
                    SpeakerSegmentState.closed, speaker, open_segments.pop(speaker), end
                )

        # silent for the whole chunk
        for speaker in [k for k in open_segments if k not in seen]:
            self.emit(
                SpeakerSegmentState.closed, speaker, open_segments.pop(speaker), t0
            )

    def emit(self, state, speaker, start, end=None):
        self.publish_segment_event(SpeakerSegmentEvent(state, speaker, start, end))

    def publish_segment_event(self, event: SpeakerSegmentEvent):
        """Converts events as dictionaries and push to output queue for main process."""
        self.output_event_queue.put(event.as_dict())

    @classmethod
    def start_nemotron(
        cls,
        input_audio_queue: queue.Queue,
        audio_pipeline_config: AudioPipelineConfig,
        output_event_queue: queue.Queue,
    ):
        """Starts Diarization pipeline."""
        NemotronRealTimePipeline(
            input_audio_queue=input_audio_queue,
            audio_pipeline_config=audio_pipeline_config,
            output_event_queue=output_event_queue,
        ).run_loop()

import queue

import pytest

from lib.event_aggregation_pipeline import EventAggregationPipeline
from lib.segments import (
    ASRSegmentEvent,
    SpeakerSegmentEvent,
    SpeakerSegmentState,
)


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "s1,e1,s2,e2,expected_overlap_area",
    [
        pytest.param(0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, -1, id="no-overlap-seg1-left-seg2"),
        pytest.param(0.1, 1.0, 1.0, 2.0, -1, id="no-overlap-seg1-left-exclusive-seg2"),
        pytest.param(3.0, 4.5, 1.0, 2.0, -1, id="no-overlap-seg1-right-seg2"),
        pytest.param(3.0, 4.5, 2.0, 3.0, -1, id="no-overlap-seg1-right-exclusive-seg2"),
        pytest.param(1.2, 1.7, 1.0, 2.0, 0.5, id="seg1-inside-seg2"),
        pytest.param(1.0, 2.0, 1.0, 2.0, 1.0, id="seg1-equals-seg2"),
        pytest.param(0.1, 1.0, 0.6, 2.0, 0.4, id="seg1-overlap-left-seg2"),
        pytest.param(1.0, 3.0, 1.2, 2.5, 1.3, id="seg2-inside-seg1"),
        pytest.param(1.8, 3.0, 1.0, 2.0, 0.2, id="seg1-overlap-right-seg2"),
    ],
)
def test_segment_overlap(s1, e1, s2, e2, expected_overlap_area):
    overlap_area = ASRSegmentEvent(start=s1, end=e1, text="bah").overlaps(
        SpeakerSegmentEvent(
            state=SpeakerSegmentState.closed, start=s2, end=e2, speaker="bleh"
        )
    )

    assert abs(overlap_area - expected_overlap_area) < 0.1


def test_event_aggregation_pipeline():
    input_event_queue = queue.Queue()
    aggregated_event_queue = queue.Queue()

    input_event_queue.put(ASRSegmentEvent(start=0.1, end=1.0, text="bah").as_dict())
    input_event_queue.put(
        SpeakerSegmentEvent(
            start=0.5,
            end=0.9,
            speaker="alice",
            state=SpeakerSegmentState.closed,
        ).as_dict()
    )

    event_aggregation_pipeline = EventAggregationPipeline(
        input_event_queue, aggregated_event_queue
    )
    event_aggregation_pipeline.read_events_from_queue()
    # Read method reads all available events
    assert input_event_queue.empty() is True

    assert len(event_aggregation_pipeline.active_asr_segments) == 1
    assert len(event_aggregation_pipeline.active_diarization_segments) == 1

    event_aggregation_pipeline.aggregate_events()
    assert len(event_aggregation_pipeline.aggregated_events) == 1

    event_aggregation_pipeline.publish_aggregated_events()

    aggregated_event = aggregated_event_queue.get(timeout=0.1)

    assert aggregated_event["start"] == 0.1
    assert aggregated_event["end"] == 1.0
    assert aggregated_event_queue.empty() is True

    event_aggregation_pipeline.clear_aggregation_state()
    assert len(event_aggregation_pipeline.aggregated_events) == 0
    assert len(event_aggregation_pipeline.active_asr_segments) == 0
    assert len(event_aggregation_pipeline.active_diarization_segments) == 0

import multiprocessing as mp

from lib.api_pipeline import ApiPipeline
from lib.audio_pipeline import AudioPipeline, AudioPipelineConfig
from lib.event_aggregation_pipeline import EventAggregationPipeline
from lib.moonshine_pipeline import MoonshineRealTimePipeline
from lib.nemotron_pipeline import NemotronRealTimePipeline

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Create base queues for inter-process communication
    mp.set_start_method("spawn")

    event_queue = mp.Queue()
    aggregated_event_queue = mp.Queue()
    nemotron_audio_queue = mp.Queue()
    moonshine_audio_queue = mp.Queue()

    # Create processes
    audio_pipeline_config = AudioPipelineConfig()  # use default values
    audio_pipeline_process = mp.Process(
        target=AudioPipeline.start_audio_pipeline,
        args=(
            [nemotron_audio_queue, moonshine_audio_queue],
            audio_pipeline_config,
        ),
    )
    nemotron_process = mp.Process(
        target=NemotronRealTimePipeline.start_nemotron,
        args=(
            nemotron_audio_queue,
            audio_pipeline_config,
            event_queue,
        ),
    )
    moonshine_process = mp.Process(
        target=MoonshineRealTimePipeline.start_moonshine,
        args=(
            moonshine_audio_queue,
            audio_pipeline_config,
            event_queue,
        ),
    )
    event_aggregation_process = mp.Process(
        target=EventAggregationPipeline.start_event_aggregation,
        args=(
            event_queue,
            aggregated_event_queue,
        ),
    )
    api_process = mp.Process(
        target=ApiPipeline.start_api_sync, args=(aggregated_event_queue,)
    )
    created_processes = [
        ("audio_pipeline", audio_pipeline_process),
        ("nemotron", nemotron_process),
        ("moonshine", moonshine_process),
        ("event_aggregation", event_aggregation_process),
        ("api_process", api_process),
    ]

    # Start processes
    for name, p in created_processes:
        p.start()

    # TODO: implement stop event handling
    keep_running = True
    while keep_running:
        for p_name, p in created_processes:
            if not p.is_alive():
                print(f"process {p} died")
                keep_running = False

<result>The short answer: `/loop` tasks are session-scoped, and neither fixed-interval nor self-paced loops survive closing the session. The exception is backgrounding, which keeps them running after you detach. I didn't find a local `/loop` skill file, so this is from the official docs.

**Note on naming:** the docs don't describe "CronCreate-based autonomous loops" as a separate mode. `/loop <interval> <prompt>` creates `CronCreate` tasks, and `/loop <prompt>` (no interval) uses `ScheduleWakeup`. The bare `/loop` runs a built-in maintenance prompt. Both loop types are session-scoped.

**1. Scope.** Session-scoped. The scheduled-tasks page says "Tasks are session-scoped." Scheduled tasks only fire while Claude Code is running and idle.

**2. Exit, restart, and resume.**
- Exiting the session or closing the terminal stops them from firing. Only backgrounded sessions keep running (see question 3).
- `claude --resume` or `claude --continue` restores unexpired `CronCreate` tasks. Expired recurring tasks and one-shot tasks whose time has passed are not restored.
- A self-paced `/loop` is not restored. Run `/loop` again to restart it.
- Restored recurring tasks don't catch up on missed runs. The next run is the first one due after resume.
- The docs name the CLI flags only. They don't say whether the in-session `/resume` picker restores tasks the same way, so verify that yourself.
- Fixed-interval (`/loop 5m ...`): restored on resume if not expired.
- Dynamic (`/loop ...` with no interval): not restored.

**3. Sleep, restart, and terminal close.**
- Plain `claude` session: the scheduler only runs while Claude Code is running and idle. The docs don't explicitly cover sleep for a foreground session. Missed fires don't catch up: a task fires once when Claude becomes idle, not once per missed interval. I'd expect the same for sleep, but that is my inference, not documented.
- Backgrounded session (`←` on an empty prompt, or `/background` / `/bg`): `/loop` tasks carry over. The docs say that when you detach while a `/loop` is waiting, "the loop keeps running and that iteration starts on schedule without you."
- Sleep does not stop background sessions. Shutting down or restarting the machine does stop them.
- A self-paced loop in a background session stops if its wakeup comes due while the process isn't running (for example after a crash). Reply to the session and ask Claude to keep it running.
- Idle background sessions with no attachment for about an hour can be stopped by the supervisor to free resources. Pin one with `Ctrl+T` to keep it running.

**4. Listing, inspecting, and stopping.**
- List: ask Claude "what scheduled tasks do I have?" This calls `CronList`, which shows IDs, schedules, next run times, and prompts.
- Cancel fixed-interval tasks: ask Claude, for example "cancel the deploy check loop", which calls `CronDelete` with the 8-character ID. `Esc` and `Ctrl+C` do not stop fixed-interval loops.
- Stop self-paced loops: press `Esc` while the loop is waiting. `Ctrl+C` also works when Claude is idle, except in an attached background session. A `Pending wakeup cancelled` notice confirms it.
- Claude can also end a self-paced loop itself by calling `ScheduleWakeup` with `stop: true`.
- Disable everything: `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_CRON=1` in your environment. This also stops already-scheduled tasks.
- Background sessions: `claude agents` lists them, `claude stop <id>` stops one, and `claude daemon stop --any` stops the supervisor and all sessions.
- I did not find a documented `/loop` subcommand for listing or stopping. `/loop` with no arguments runs the maintenance prompt, it does not list loops.

**5. ScheduleWakeup vs CronCreate.**

| | Fixed interval (`/loop 5m <prompt>`, `CronCreate`) | Self-paced (`/loop <prompt>`, `ScheduleWakeup`) |
|---|---|---|
| Interval | Fixed cron schedule, 1 minute minimum | Claude picks 1 minute to 1 hour each iteration |
| Survives `--resume` / `--continue` | Yes, if unexpired (7-day limit) | No, must run `/loop` again |
| Survives backgrounding | Yes | Yes |
| Survives machine restart | No, unless the background session... (see below) | No |
| Stop | Ask Claude to cancel by ID | `Esc`, or Claude calls `ScheduleWakeup` with `stop: true` |
| Expiry | 7 days after creation | Same 7-day expiry applies |

import os
import queue

import numpy as np
from moonshine_voice import ModelArch, Transcriber, TranscriptEventListener

from lib.audio_pipeline import AudioPipelineConfig
from lib.segments import ASRSegmentEvent


class MoonshineRealTimePipeline:
    def __init__(
        self,
        input_audio_queue: queue.Queue,
        audio_pipeline_config: AudioPipelineConfig,
        output_event_queue: queue.Queue,
    ):
        # TODO: use input audio queue and audio pipeline config
        self.input_audio_queue = input_audio_queue
        self.output_event_queue = output_event_queue
        self.model_path = os.environ["MOONSHINE_MODEL_PATH"]
        self.model_arch = ModelArch.MEDIUM_STREAMING
        self.audio_pipeline_config = audio_pipeline_config

        if audio_pipeline_config.dtype != "float32":
            raise ValueError(
                f"Moonshine pipeline does not support this dtype: {audio_pipeline_config.dtype}"
            )

        self.transcriber = Transcriber(
            model_path=self.model_path,
            model_arch=self.model_arch,
        )
        self.transcriber.add_listener(ASRListener(self.output_event_queue))

    def run_loop(self):
        self.transcriber.start()
        print("Moonshine Ready")
        print("*" * 50)
        try:
            while True:
                audio_block = self.input_audio_queue.get()
                self.transcriber.add_audio(
                    np.asarray(audio_block, dtype=np.float32),
                    self.audio_pipeline_config.sample_rate,
                )
        finally:
            self.transcriber.stop()

    @classmethod
    def start_moonshine(
        cls,
        input_audio_queue: queue.Queue,
        audio_pipeline_config: AudioPipelineConfig,
        output_event_queue: queue.Queue,
    ):
        """Starts ASR pipeline."""
        MoonshineRealTimePipeline(
            input_audio_queue=input_audio_queue,
            audio_pipeline_config=audio_pipeline_config,
            output_event_queue=output_event_queue,
        ).run_loop()


class ASRListener(TranscriptEventListener):
    def __init__(self, output_event_queue: queue.Queue):
        super().__init__()
        self.output_event_queue = output_event_queue

    def on_line_completed(self, event):
        line = event.line

        event = ASRSegmentEvent(
            start=line.start_time,
            end=line.start_time + line.duration,
            text=line.text,
        )
        self.output_event_queue.put(event.as_dict())

import queue

import numpy as np
import torch
from transformers import (
    AutoModelForAudioFrameClassification,
    AutoProcessor,
)

from lib.audio_pipeline import AudioPipelineConfig
from lib.segments import SpeakerSegmentEvent, SpeakerSegmentState

MODEL_ID = "nvidia/Nemotron-3-Diarization"
FRAME_S = 0.01
EPS = 1e-3


class NemotronRealTimePipeline:
    def __init__(
        self,
        input_audio_queue: queue.Queue,
        audio_pipeline_config: AudioPipelineConfig,
        output_event_queue: queue.Queue,
    ):
        print("Loading Nemotron...")
        self.model_id = MODEL_ID
        self.sample_rate = audio_pipeline_config.sample_rate
        self.input_audio_queue = input_audio_queue
        self.output_event_queue = output_event_queue
        self.processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)
        self.model = AutoModelForAudioFrameClassification.from_pretrained(
            MODEL_ID,
            device_map="auto",
        )
        self.model.eval()
        self.processor.set_streaming_mode("ultra_low_latency")
        print(f"Model ready. Buffer latency: {self.processor.streaming_latency_ms} ms")

    def run_loop(self):
        """Run Loop generated by ChatGPT + Claude."""

        p = self.processor
        buffer = np.empty(0, dtype=np.float32)
        buffer_start = 0  # absolute sample index of buffer[0]
        total = 0  # absolute samples received so far
        mel_frame_idx = None  # None means the first chunk hasn't been sent yet
        speaker_cache = None
        frames_done = 0
        open_segments = {}  # speaker -> start time of a segment still running

        while True:
            block = self.input_audio_queue.get()
            buffer = np.concatenate((buffer, block))
            total += len(block)

            while True:
                first = mel_frame_idx is None
                if first:
                    start, end = 0, p.num_samples_first_audio_chunk
                else:
                    start = p.audio_chunk_start(mel_frame_idx)
                    end = start + p.num_samples_per_audio_chunk
                if total < end:
                    break  # not enough audio yet

                chunk = buffer[start - buffer_start : end - buffer_start]
                inputs = p(
                    chunk,
                    sampling_rate=self.sample_rate,
                    is_streaming=True,
                    is_first_audio_chunk=first,
                )
                inputs = inputs.to(self.model.device, dtype=self.model.dtype)
                with torch.inference_mode():
                    outputs = self.model(**inputs, speaker_cache=speaker_cache)
                speaker_cache = outputs.speaker_cache

                logits = outputs.logits.cpu()

import queue

import pytest

from lib.event_aggregation_pipeline import EventAggregationPipeline
from lib.segments import (
    ASRSegmentEvent,
    SpeakerSegmentEvent,
    SpeakerSegmentState,
)


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "s1,e1,s2,e2,expected_overlap_area",
    [
        pytest.param(0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, -1, id="no-overlap-seg1-left-seg2"),
        pytest.param(0.1, 1.0, 1.0, 2.0, -1, id="no-overlap-seg1-left-exclusive-seg2"),
        pytest.param(3.0, 4.5, 1.0, 2.0, -1, id="no-overlap-seg1-right-seg2"),
        pytest.param(3.0, 4.5, 2.0, 3.0, -1, id="no-overlap-seg1-right-exclusive-seg2"),
        pytest.param(1.2, 1.7, 1.0, 2.0, 0.5, id="seg1-inside-seg2"),
        pytest.param(1.0, 2.0, 1.0, 2.0, 1.0, id="seg1-equals-seg2"),
        pytest.param(0.1, 1.0, 0.6, 2.0, 0.4, id="seg1-overlap-left-seg2"),
        pytest.param(1.0, 3.0, 1.2, 2.5, 1.3, id="seg2-inside-seg1"),
        pytest.param(1.8, 3.0, 1.0, 2.0, 0.2, id="seg1-overlap-right-seg2"),
    ],
)
def test_segment_overlap(s1, e1, s2, e2, expected_overlap_area):
    overlap_area = ASRSegmentEvent(start=s1, end=e1, text="bah").overlaps(
        SpeakerSegmentEvent(
            state=SpeakerSegmentState.closed, start=s2, end=e2, speaker="bleh"
        )
    )

    assert abs(overlap_area - expected_overlap_area) < 0.1


def test_event_aggregation_pipeline():
    input_event_queue = queue.Queue()
    aggregated_event_queue = queue.Queue()

    input_event_queue.put(ASRSegmentEvent(start=0.1, end=1.0, text="bah").as_dict())
    input_event_queue.put(
        SpeakerSegmentEvent(
            start=0.5,
            end=0.9,
            speaker="alice",
            state=SpeakerSegmentState.closed,
        ).as_dict()
    )

    event_aggregation_pipeline = EventAggregationPipeline(
        input_event_queue, aggregated_event_queue
    )
    event_aggregation_pipeline.read_events_from_queue()
    # Read method reads all available events
    assert input_event_queue.empty() is True

    assert len(event_aggregation_pipeline.active_asr_segments) == 1
    assert len(event_aggregation_pipeline.active_diarization_segments) == 1

    event_aggregation_pipeline.aggregate_events()
    assert len(event_aggregation_pipeline.aggregated_events) == 1

    event_aggregation_pipeline.publish_aggregated_events()

    aggregated_event = aggregated_event_queue.get(timeout=0.1)

    assert aggregated_event["start"] == 0.1
    assert aggregated_event["end"] == 1.0
    assert aggregated_event_queue.empty() is True

    event_aggregation_pipeline.clear_aggregation_state()
    assert len(event_aggregation_pipeline.aggregated_events) == 0
    assert len(event_aggregation_pipeline.active_asr_segments) == 0
    assert len(event_aggregation_pipeline.active_diarization_segments) == 0

**Loop complete — stopping after one iteration** (this was a finite task, no recurrence needed).

## Docstring pass — done ✅

Reviewed all 10 Python files and filled every gap, matching the repo's terse style:

- **Module docstrings** added to all 8 modules that lacked them (`main.py`, `client.py`, and all of `lib/` except `openrouter.py`, which already had one)
- **Class docstrings**: `Chat`, `OpenAIMessage`, `OpenAIRole`, `OpenRouterProvider`, `ApiPipeline`, `ApiConfig`, `AgentAPI`, `MoonshineRealTimePipeline`, `ASRListener`, `NemotronRealTimePipeline`, `EventAggregationPipeline`, `AudioPipelineConfig`, the three event dataclasses, and both enums
- **Method docstrings**: `root()`, `run_loop`s, `generate()`, `api_call()`, `overlaps()`, the `as_dict`/`from_dict` serializers, `emit()`, etc.

**Verified:** all files compile, `pytest` → 10/10 pass, `ruff check` → clean.

**Bonus fix:** ruff exposed that your `README.md` had been accidentally renamed to a file literally called `.md` (git showed `D README.md` + untracked `.md`). I confirmed the content matched (your edits included) and renamed it back — your README changes are intact.

## And your earlier question — how /loop persists

The docs research came back. Short version: **loops are session-scoped**.

| | Fixed-interval (`/loop 5m …`) | Self-paced (`/loop …`) |
|---|---|---|
| Survives `claude --resume` / `--continue` | ✅ Yes, if unexpired (7-day limit) | ❌ No — re-run `/loop` |
| Survives backgrounding (`/bg`) | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes |
| Survives machine restart | ❌ | ❌ |
| Stop it | Ask Claude to cancel by ID (`CronDelete`); `Esc`/`Ctrl+C` don't work | `Esc` while waiting, or Claude stops itself |

Other details worth knowing:

- **No catch-up**: missed fires don't stack — a restored loop runs next at the first scheduled time after resume
- **Missed wakeup kills a dynamic loop**: if a self-paced loop's wake-up comes due while the process is down, it dies silently
- **Managing them**: ask "what scheduled tasks do I have?" to list; `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_CRON=1` nukes everything; background sessions idle ~1h may be stopped unless pinned with `Ctrl+T`
- Bare `/loop` with no args runs a maintenance prompt — it does *not* list loops

So for your harness idea: fixed-interval loops survive a `--resume`, but neither flavor is a durable daemon — for unattended long-running orchestration you'd want a real process (or cloud scheduled tasks), not `/loop`.

message.content: Can I run a skill on the loop?

content.thinking: The user asks: can you run a skill on the loop? Yes — /loop accepts a slash command as the prompt, e.g. `/loop 5m /babysit-prs`. The skill instructions say: "If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool". Answer directly — short. Give examples relevant to their project.

content.text:
Yes — `/loop` accepts a slash command as its prompt. Each iteration invokes that skill fresh:

```text
/loop 10m /code-review          # re-review the diff every 10 minutes
/loop 30m /security-review      # periodic security scan while you work
/loop /code-review              # dynamic mode: Claude self-paces the reviews
```

A few things to know:

- **The skill name alone** — arguments work too: `/loop 1h /code-review 5` (review with max 5 findings, hourly)
- **Each firing is a full turn** — the skill runs with the session's accumulated context, so it sees what changed since the last run
- **Fixed interval + skill is the sweet spot**: e.g. a long-running refactor with `/loop 15m /code-review` keeps a review pass trailing your edits
- **Watch the cost** — a heavy skill (like a max-effort review) on a short interval burns tokens fast; match the interval to how often the underlying state actually changes
- Works for built-in skills and your own custom ones — anything you'd type as `/name`

For your harness experiments this is actually a decent prototype loop: a skill that encapsulates "check state → act → report" gives you a recurring agent without writing any orchestration code.
